metadata.note: deep-explainer, fresh technical build covering CI/CD and deployment practices on GCP: GitHub Actions, Pull Requests, dev/staging/production environments, Docker, Kubernetes (importance + GKE setup), and the three deployment strategies (Rolling/Blue-Green/Canary) with use cases, pros, and cons. 4 acts: I GitHub Actions + PRs (the gate), II environments (the promotion path), III Docker + Kubernetes (package + orchestrate; GKE setup), IV deployment strategies (how you actually ship). Content is general, well-established DevOps/cloud engineering practice -- deliberately hedged away from version numbers, pricing, or GCP console screenshots per DOUBLE-CHECK LAW (see FACTCHECK.md). No Manim on this machine (pangocairo not installed) -- MANIM lane absorbed into REMOTION. VOX quota: 5 real Wikimedia Commons photographs, metaphor imagery. BinaryBranch/DivergentFates hero beats planned up front at A1-4, A2-3, A2-5, A4-3, A4-4 for clean 9:16 Short derivation. Signed for Divyank from authoring time. GATE P: PENDING, see PEDAGOGY.md.

beats.act: cold open
beats.narration_text: Salaam — this is Liam, in for Divyank. A pull request that passes every review can still break production the moment it deploys — because merging code and shipping code are two completely different problems, solved by two completely different systems. Let's build the whole pipeline, GCP-shaped, end to end.

beats.act: Act II — Three Environments, One Path
beats.narration_text: The same build gets handed off three times before it ever reaches a real user — and the whole discipline is refusing to rebuild it at each handoff.

beats.act: Act II — Three Environments, One Path
beats.narration_text: Dev: fast, disposable, breaks constantly, and that's fine. Staging: a production-like environment, the last real check before real users are ever at risk. Production: real traffic, the strictest gate of the three — the only one a customer actually feels.

beats.act: Act II — Three Environments, One Path
beats.narration_text: Rebuild the container at every environment, or promote the exact same image forward. Rebuilding risks a different artifact reaching production than the one staging actually tested. Promoting the same image is the only way the test that passed is the thing that ships.

beats.act: Act III — Containers and Orchestration
beats.narration_text: Docker packages the application with everything it actually needs to run — the runtime, the libraries, the exact versions — into one immutable image. Ship the image, not a list of setup instructions somebody has to follow correctly by hand.

beats.act: Act III — Containers and Orchestration
beats.narration_text: One container is easy. Thousands of them, scheduled across machines, restarted the moment they crash, is an orchestration problem — and that's exactly the job Kubernetes exists to do.

shot.prompt: real archival air-traffic-control photo -- illustrative of Kubernetes orchestration, not a literal depiction. Already sourced, see media/A3-4.source.txt

beats.act: Act III — Containers and Orchestration
beats.narration_text: Kubernetes' actual job: schedule containers onto available machines, restart the ones that crash, scale the count up or down under load, and route traffic to whichever pods are actually healthy right now. On GCP, concretely: a GKE cluster, kubectl pointed at it, a Deployment and a Service defined in YAML, then applied.

Define: a Deployment and a Service in YAML
Apply — Kubernetes takes it from there

beats.act: Act III — Containers and Orchestration
beats.narration_text: Autopilot, or Standard? Autopilot: Google manages the nodes, you manage workloads only, less control. Standard: you manage the node pools directly yourself, full control, more operational work. Both run the exact same Kubernetes API underneath.

beats.act: Act IV — How You Actually Ship It
beats.narration_text: Even with a tested image and a running cluster, one decision is still yours: how new code actually replaces old code, while real users are on the line.

beats.act: Act IV — How You Actually Ship It
beats.narration_text: Three real strategies. Rolling: replace old pods with new ones gradually — the Kubernetes default. Blue-Green: run two complete environments, switch all traffic at once. Canary: send a small slice of real traffic to the new version first, and watch it before committing further.

show.event: three chips snap in: Rolling, Blue-Green, Canary

items: Rolling — gradual pod replacement, the K8s default
Blue-Green — two full environments, one instant switch
Canary — a small slice of real traffic, watched first
props.caption: same tested image, three ways to expose it

beats.act: Act IV — How You Actually Ship It
beats.narration_text: Rolling's honest tradeoff: no extra infrastructure, no downtime, built into Kubernetes natively. But old and new versions serve real traffic side by side during the rollout, and there's no single-switch instant rollback.

beats.act: Act IV — How You Actually Ship It
beats.narration_text: Blue-Green's honest tradeoff: one switch, and rollback is exactly as instant — flip straight back to blue. But you're running double the infrastructure during the cutover, and a database migration doesn't get to enjoy that same instant rollback.

beats.act: Act IV — How You Actually Ship It
beats.narration_text: Canary's honest tradeoff: real production traffic validates the new version before most users ever see it, catching what staging couldn't. But it needs real traffic-splitting infrastructure and real metrics — without both, a canary is just a rolling deploy wearing a fancier name.

beats.act: verdict
beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. GitHub Actions is the automated gate, pull requests are the human one — branch protection makes the automated check mandatory, not a comment somebody has to remember to read. Dev, staging, and production exist to catch different failure classes in order, and the whole discipline is build once, promote the same image forward, never rebuild at the gate. Docker makes the artifact identical everywhere it runs; Kubernetes schedules, restarts, scales, and routes traffic to thousands of those containers — set up on GCP as a GKE cluster, a Deployment, and a Service. And Rolling, Blue-Green, and Canary trade off differently: no extra infrastructure, versus instant rollback, versus real-traffic validation — pick based on which failure you can least afford, not which one sounds most advanced.

show.event: four artifact lines stagger in, one per act

artifactLines: GitHub Actions is the automated gate, pull requests are the human one — branch protection makes the check mandatory, not a comment to remember.
Dev/staging/production catch different failure classes in order; the discipline is build once, promote the same image forward, never rebuild at the gate.
Docker makes the artifact identical everywhere; Kubernetes schedules/restarts/scales/routes it at scale — set up on GCP as a GKE cluster, a Deployment, a Service.
Rolling, Blue-Green, and Canary trade off no-extra-infra vs. instant-rollback vs. real-traffic-validation — pick the failure you can least afford.
